_note: City-level youthful-active-lifestyle scores, one per law-school city. This replaces the old state-level 'community' score because lifestyle varies enormously within a state (Austin vs. Lubbock). Sub-signals are 1-5: social = nightlife/dining/music/young-professional density (weighted heaviest); outdoors = active outdoor recreation; walkability = walkable/transit vs. car-dependent. lifestyleScore = 0.5*social + 0.25*outdoors + 0.25*walkability, rounded to the nearest 0.5. Editable estimates, not survey data. lat/lon: US Census 2024 Gazetteer place interior points, with a few hand-placed where the city isn't a Census place (NYC boroughs, New England towns) or its interior point misleads (San Francisco, Portland ME, Orlando, New York).

cities.blurb: A village of about 5,000 built around the university. Essentially no independent social scene — this is a heads-down three years.
Cheap rust-belt city with surprisingly good outdoors in Cuyahoga Valley National Park just north. Thin nightlife; Cleveland is 40 minutes.
State-capital town with a modest but real scene, a student presence, and easy access to the Adirondacks and Berkshires.
Sandia Mountains on one side, the Rio Grande bosque on the other, and 300 days of sun. Cheap, gritty, and thoroughly car-dependent.
Quintessential vibrant college town — walkable, foodie, young, and cultured around the University of Michigan. Small, but punches above its size.
Legendary music-scene college town (UGA) — walkable, cheap, and young. Small, but a lot of fun for its size.
A major young-professional and cultural hub with nightlife, music, and diversity. Sprawl and traffic are the price of admission.
The poster child for youthful and active — live music, lakes and greenbelts, food trucks, and a young, growing crowd. Traffic and rising costs are the downside.
A purpose-built town of a few thousand in the Southwest Florida farmland. Nearly no independent social scene; Naples is 30 minutes away.
An underrated, affordable arts/music/food city with walkable rowhouse neighborhoods and harbor access. Crime and blight in pockets are real.
LSU-driven and affordable, with New Orleans an hour away for anything the city can't supply. Hot, humid, and car-dependent.
Bustling university town with Bay Area access, a walkable core, and hills/bay trails close by. Young and active, though pricey.
Cheap, and the food-and-music scene punches above the metro's size. Sprawling and car-first once you leave Avondale or Five Points.
Unusually good college town — live music, a compact walkable core, and Hoosier National Forest nearby. Cheap, and it empties in summer.
One of the most student-dense cities in the country — walkable, transit-rich, packed with bars, sports, and young professionals. Expensive and cold.
About as outdoors-forward as American cities get — trailheads at the edge of a compact, walkable, bike-mad downtown. Expensive and small.
Small waterfront town on Narragansett Bay with sailing and the East Bay Bike Path. Providence is 30 minutes for anything else.
The epicenter of young, creative NYC — endless food, nightlife, and arts, all walkable and transit-connected. Very expensive.
Affordable, revitalizing rust-belt city with a growing food scene and real neighborhood character. Long, snowy winters.
Harvard/MIT energy: cafes, bookstores, and a young academic crowd on foot and transit. Pricey and small.
Working waterfront city directly across from Philadelphia, which is where the social life is — PATCO gets you there in minutes.
Small, remote southern-Illinois university town with nearby Shawnee forest but a thin nightlife scene.
Small, walkable historic borough in the Cumberland Valley with the Appalachian Trail close by. Cheap and very quiet.
Suburban Long Island hamlet — commuter-oriented and car-dependent, with a limited youthful scene of its own.
Lively UIUC college-town energy and a walkable campus core, but marooned in central-Illinois cornfields.
Classic Tar Heel college town — walkable Franklin Street, young, and lively, with Triangle amenities nearby.
Historic, coastal, and genuinely fun — a celebrated food scene, beaches, and a walkable core. Tourist crowds and heat are the tradeoffs.
Blue Ridge and Shenandoah on the doorstep, a walkable downtown mall, and a strong wine-and-food scene. Small and not cheap.
World-class dining, nightlife, and culture with a lakefront full of running paths and beaches, all on excellent transit. Winters are the tax.
Over-the-Rhine is one of the better walkable nightlife districts in the Midwest, and housing is cheap. Hilly, with good river access.
Very cheap, with world-class cultural institutions, lakefront access, and the Metroparks 'Emerald Necklace.' Winters are grey and long.
Mid-Missouri college town with good trail access (the Katy Trail) and a walkable downtown. Cheap and comfortably scaled.
State-capital college town (USC) with steady student energy and affordability, but hot summers and a modest scene.
Young, growing, and cheap, with the Short North supplying most of the nightlife. Flat and bikeable; outdoors is unremarkable.
Small, quiet capital with the White Mountains and Lakes Region within easy reach. Very little in the way of nightlife.
Upscale, leafy Miami-area city with a walkable Miracle Mile and quick access to Miami's scene and beaches. Pricey.
Big-city dining, nightlife, and sports with a large young-professional base, but sprawling and very car-dependent.
Coastal southeastern-Massachusetts town near New Bedford — quiet, with limited youthful nightlife.
Suburban, horse-country-adjacent Broward County. Beaches and the Everglades are close, but you will drive everywhere.
Flat, bike-obsessed college town — great for an active outdoor routine, but a quiet nightlife scene and isolated from a big city.
Inexpensive, with an excellent regional bike-trail network and river access. Small social scene, largely car-dependent.
Quiet NIU college town west of Chicago — affordable and small, with a limited youthful scene.
Young, active, and beer-soaked, with the Front Range an hour west. Downtown walks well; the rest sprawls. No longer cheap.
Underrated small capital — cheap, walkable downtown, strong trail network, and a real young-professional cohort in the East Village.
A revitalizing city with a real arts, music, and dining renaissance at low cost. Gritty in spots and light on outdoors.
Reinvented tobacco town turned foodie/arts hub with a young, creative Research Triangle crowd. Rising fast.
Michigan State college-town energy with a walkable strip and decent outdoors, but modest beyond campus life.
Track Town — running, cycling, and river trails everywhere, with the Cascades and coast both an hour out. Small, wet, and cheap for Oregon.
Northern Virginia suburb with Metro access into DC, which supplies the actual social life. Expensive for what it is.
Ozarks trail town with a genuinely good mountain-biking network and a lively square. Cheap, growing, and much younger than the state average.
Friendlier, more laid-back DFW alternative with a growing scene, but quieter nightlife than Dallas and car-dependent.
Energetic Gator college town with springs and trails nearby — young, affordable, and lively during the school year.
Very small, very cheap, and very cold. A compact downtown and river greenway; the social scene is almost entirely campus.
Mid-size Piedmont city with a modest college scene and affordable living — pleasant but not buzzing.
A town of about 1,000 deep in the Appalachian coalfields. Outstanding hiking and ATV trails; essentially no social infrastructure.
Small artsy Gulf-coast enclave near St. Pete/Tampa — beaches and a quirky scene, but modest nightlife of its own.
Small capital on the Susquehanna with a compact riverfront core. Cheap, practical, and limited after hours.
Insurance-industry capital that empties out on weekends. Cheap for the Northeast, with easy rail to Boston and New York when you need more.
Long Island hub near Hofstra with LIRR access to NYC, but the immediate area is suburban and modest.
Northern Kentucky campus suburb across the river from Cincinnati, which supplies most of the actual nightlife. Car-dependent and cheap.
Unmatched outdoors — surf, reef, and ridge hikes inside the city limits. Small legal market, extreme cost of living, and a long flight from anywhere.
Enormous, diverse dining and nightlife and a young workforce, offset by heat, humidity, sprawl, and limited outdoors.
Affordable, flat, and very bikeable along the Cultural Trail. Growing food scene; still a car city outside the Mile Square.
A literary college town with a genuinely walkable pedestrian mall and outsized bar and arts density for its size. Very cheap.
Master-planned, spotless, and safe with beaches and trails nearby, but sterile and car-dependent with little organic young-adult scene.
Gorges, lakes, and trails everywhere around Cornell — a small, outdoorsy, youthful town, if an isolated and snowy one.
Small, very cheap capital with a limited social scene and real infrastructure problems. Car-dependent.
Sprawling, cheap by Florida standards, with genuine beach and St. Johns River access. The urban core is thin and very car-dependent.
Barbecue, jazz, and a legitimately good restaurant scene at a fraction of coastal cost. Sprawling, though the streetcar core is improving.
Vols college town at the gateway to the Smokies — strong outdoors, a reviving downtown, and low cost.
State-capital town with a steady, low-key scene and affordable living — youthful energy is moderate.
High-plains town at 7,200 feet with the Snowy Range and Vedauwoo minutes away. Tiny, windy, cheap, and cold.
Enormous nightlife if you want it, and Red Rock and Mount Charleston for when you don't. Extremely car-dependent and brutally hot.
Massachusetts Street is one of the better small-city main drags in the Midwest — live music, bars, and everything walkable. Cheap and young.
Horse country with a compact, improving downtown and good cycling on the surrounding rolling roads. Affordable and manageable.
Tiny, handsome Shenandoah Valley town with immediate access to the Blue Ridge and the Maury River. Very quiet.
Affordable, safe, bike-friendly capital with a Husker-driven social calendar. Compact downtown; not much beyond it.
Affordable capital with a walkable River Market district and trail access along the Arkansas River. Limited beyond that, and car-dependent.
Endless dining, nightlife, beaches, and hiking, with a huge young population. The catch is sprawl — you live in your car.
Cheap, distinctive, and genuinely fun — bourbon, the Highlands, and a strong independent-restaurant streak. Waterfront and park access is good.
Isolated West Texas college town centered on Texas Tech — affordable, but a limited youthful/active scene.
Small Blue Ridge foothills city with river and trail access. Limited nightlife; conservative and car-dependent.
Small Central Georgia city with historic charm and affordability, but a limited youthful/active scene.
An isthmus between two lakes, a walkable State Street, and an exceptional bike network. One of the best college-town lifestyles anywhere.
Stunning beaches and canyon trails, but isolated, wealthy, and older — essentially no walkable nightlife or young social scene.
Deep music and food culture at very low cost, with real grit — crime and limited outdoors are the downsides.
Iconic nightlife, beaches, and an international young crowd with year-round outdoor life. Expensive, hot, and sprawling.
North-county Miami suburb near Hard Rock Stadium — quiet and car-dependent, but with metro Miami within reach.
Cheap, with a strong bar and festival culture and real Lake Michigan access. Winters are hard; the city is very segregated.
Lakes, an elite bike network, and real theater and music — one of the best active-lifestyle cities in the country if you can take the winter.
River running through downtown, trailheads at the edge of town, and a small but real music scene. Isolated, and increasingly not cheap.
Small capital with a serious civil-rights heritage but a thin nightlife bench. Car-dependent, inexpensive, quiet after dark.
Mountaineer town on the Monongahela with whitewater, climbing, and the rail-trail network close. Cheap, hilly, and football-driven.
Palouse college town with immediate access to hills, rivers, and the Idaho backcountry. Tiny, isolated, and very cheap.
A booming magnet for young people — music, nightlife, and food everywhere. Growth has brought traffic and rising rents.
Dense, walkable, and far livelier than its reputation — a real pizza and music town. Long Island Sound and East Rock are close.
Nowhere else has this much social life per dollar. Walkable, musical, and cheap; also hot, hurricane-exposed, and hard on a study schedule.
The ultimate walkable, transit-rich, always-on city — unmatched dining, nightlife, and young energy. Cost of living is the obstacle.
Transit-rich and cheap for the region, with Manhattan 20 minutes by train. Improving downtown; limited outdoors.
Leafy, safe Boston suburb on the T — comfortable and connected, but sedate rather than youthful.
OU college town with a walkable Campus Corner and a football-shaped social calendar. Very cheap; Oklahoma City is 25 minutes.
Quiet suburb north of New Haven. Car-dependent and residential; the actual social life is a ten-minute drive away.
Cheap and rapidly redeveloping, with Bricktown and the Scissortail Park boathouse district. Sprawling and car-first.
Bigger and more varied than Lincoln, with the Old Market for walkable nightlife. Cheap, steady, and quietly comfortable.
Solid Orange County base with beaches and an old-town core, but largely suburban and car-dependent.
Theme-park city with a young workforce and a growing nightlife/dining scene, offset by heavy sprawl and tourism.
The Square gives Oxford an outsized bar-and-bookstore culture for a town this small. Very cheap; isolated and football-seasonal.
Dense, walkable, transit-rich, and much cheaper than New York or Boston — one of the strongest big-city values on this list.
Cheap, hilly, and genuinely walkable neighborhood by neighborhood, with three rivers and good trail access. Underrated food scene.
A small city with a wildly disproportionate food scene, a walkable Old Port, and the coast and mountains both close. Winters are long.
Bikeable, walkable, and hemmed in by the Gorge, Mount Hood, and the coast. Excellent food and beer; grey for eight months.
Wasatch Front canyons and world-class skiing minutes away, paired with a notably quiet nightlife scene given the local culture.
The most diverse place in America — incredible food, dense neighborhoods, and NYC access at a (relative) discount.
Fast-growing capital drawing young professionals, with a good food/beer scene and Triangle access. Car-oriented overall.
The James River runs whitewater straight through downtown — rare for a city this size. Cheap, creative, and quickly improving.
Cheaper than the Bay with a real farm-to-table scene and river/delta access. Tahoe is two hours out; summers run hot.
Quieter, more residential twin with a handsome walkable core and river bluffs. Minneapolis nightlife is a short light-rail ride away.
Quiet capital in the Willamette Valley, with wine country and the Cascades nearby. Social life is thin — Portland is an hour north.
Hard to beat for outdoors — seven ski resorts within an hour and canyon trailheads from downtown. Compact grid, growing food scene.
River Walk energy and a solid food scene, family-friendly and affordable, though the young-professional nightlife is modest.
Beach city with perfect weather and a genuinely active outdoor culture, plus a real nightlife scene. Some neighborhoods walkable, most not.
Dense, transit-rich, and stacked with dining/nightlife plus quick outdoor escapes — a magnet for young professionals. Brutally expensive.
Heart of Silicon Valley with a young tech workforce, but suburban and car-dependent with a thin nightlife scene.
Mountains, water, and forest in every direction, with a dense walkable core and real transit. Expensive, and dark from November to March.
Small, cheap, and heavily oriented around Notre Dame. Lake Michigan is an hour; the winters are long.
A village of a few hundred in the White River valley. Exceptional hiking, skiing, and paddling; effectively no nightlife at all.
Cheap for the Northwest, with the Spokane River through downtown and skiing 45 minutes out. Small but improving social scene.
Western-Massachusetts city that's affordable but economically strained, with a limited young-adult scene.
Cheap housing, big-city cultural institutions, and Forest Park. Uneven neighborhood by neighborhood, and mostly car-dependent.
Beautiful, affluent, and outdoorsy on the Peninsula, but a quiet campus-bubble feel rather than a nightlife town.
Central New York college town (SU) with steady student energy and affordability, but famously long, snowy winters.
FSU capital college town — youthful during the year, with trails and lakes nearby, but sleepy otherwise.
Dense, young ASU energy on Mill Avenue with light rail into Phoenix. Desert hiking is minutes away; summers are brutal.
Cheap, quiet, and industrial, with Lake Erie and the Maumee close by. Detroit and Ann Arbor are both under an hour.
Small, very affordable capital with a quiet social scene. Kansas City is an hour east when you need more.
Cheap desert college town ringed by four mountain ranges — exceptional hiking and cycling. Social scene is modest and student-driven.
Art-deco downtown, a strong park system along the Arkansas River, and cheap housing. Modest but real nightlife.
A football town — enormous social energy on fall weekends, much quieter otherwise. The Black Warrior River and Lake Tuscaloosa are close.
A town of about 11,000 on the Missouri River bluffs. Almost entirely campus-driven; extremely cheap and extremely quiet.
Main Line suburb with a regional-rail stop into Center City Philadelphia. Leafy and quiet; the nightlife is 30 minutes east.
Oceanfront living with year-round surf, paddling, and the Back Bay refuge. Sprawling, seasonal, and thoroughly car-dependent.
Small Central Texas city built around Baylor — quiet, affordable, with limited nightlife and a mostly student social life.
Dense, transit-rich, and packed with young professionals — the single best city in the country for a policy-minded law student. Expensive, and the pace is relentless.
Compact Westchester downtown with some dining/nightlife and Metro-North straight into NYC — convenient but suburban.
Colonial-historic and walkable in its small core, with the York River and Jamestown nearby. Very quiet outside William & Mary.
Corporate-law company town with a compact riverfront core. Philadelphia is 30 minutes by train, which is where most weekends go.
Arts-district charm and affordability in the Triad, but a quieter, smaller-city pace.
